catalog_quote: In UT there are two verb classes that consistently condition allomorphy in suffixes that immediately attach to them: Class I conditions lenis allomorphs and Class II conditions fortis allomorphs. Also verbs of class I condition allomorphy depending on whether or not the verb root bears primary stress. There is no way to predict which class a verb belongs to based on its phonological form: verbs in both classes may be of 2, 3, and 4 syllables in length, and may bear stress on any of these syllables, and may end with the same inventory of vowels. ... new_statements.quote: [p. 7] Stress occurs on every word and is phonemic. There is also a phrase stress which does not necessarily co-occur with word stress and thus far is limited to specific morphemes. [p. 60] In all of the two syllable roots, when the locative -či is added to the root, the stress shifts to the -či, with the exceptions of gupá 'hair' and elá 'blood', which keep the stress on the second syllable. [p. 102] In the second group, the stress which was on the stem shifts to the first syllable of the future suffix: yawí 'dance' becomes yawi-méa 'will dance'. In the first group, the stress remains on the stem: ená 'walk' becomes ená-ma 'will walk'.

new_statements.relation_note: The p. 7 sentence is already the catalog's domain_quote for lowl1265 (classification lexical, main quote from Valdez Jara 2013), so on placement type it agrees. New here: the morphology sections give the lexical-class stress shifts with named lexical exceptions (locative -či, possessive -la, -ma vs -mea future classes, plural stems), which correspond to Valdez Jara's Class 1 'keep / do not keep primary stress' roots and add exceptions the catalog does not list. Nothing on window, weight or default position. The catalog's open_url (sil.org/acpub/repository/) is dead and sil.org/resources/archives/18497 is now an unrelated item; the volume is SIL archive record 8451, file.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Every word carries one stress and stress is phonemic (contrastive); no positional, weight or window rule is given anywhere in the sketch. Stress placement in derived and inflected words is set by lexical class: the locative -či pulls stress onto itself in disyllabic body-part roots (two named exceptions), -la/-lači keep root stress except in five listed roots; verbs split into a -ma future class that keeps stem stress and a -mea/-méa class in which stress moves to the first syllable of the future suffix (and 'shifts for other suffixes also'); some plural stems differ from singulars by a stress shift. Compounds carry a single accent; clitics are stressed when they act as words and unstressed when they act as affixes.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary word stress mentioned. A separate 'phrase stress', 'limited to specific morphemes', is said to be carried often by the emphatic suffixes -'e, -če and -go (pp. 18-19, 42-43). Section on p. 8 refers only to stressed vs nonstressed syllables (pre-glottal transitional vocoid in stressed syllables, vowel loss and open allophone of i in nonstressed syllables) and refers the compiler to Burgess 1970 'Tarahumara Phonology' for more detail.
new_statements.exceptions: gupá 'hair' and elá 'blood' keep second-syllable stress when locative -či is added; elá, ramé, siwá, wemá, iná shift stress when -la / -lači are added (p. 60); the clitic =ne 'I' 'sometimes carries stress and sometimes does not' after a verb (p. 101); go'a/go'-méa 'eat' is the one -mea-class stem not ending in u or unstressed i (p. 103).
new_statements.identity_note: Both Burgess works describe Western Tarahumara as spoken in the Urique-Oteros-Chínipas canyon triangle, SW Chihuahua: fieldsite Rocoroibo, main consultant Albino Mares Trías of Bacusinare (mun. Guazapares); the phonology was analysed in 1968 with Encarnación Velasquillo under Eunice Pike and published as Burgess 1970 'Tarahumara Phonology (Rocoroibo dialect)' (still not open: ERIC ED038653 has no full text, archive.org isbn_874040191 is lending-only). This is Glottolog lowl1265 / ISO tac; Valdez Jara's Urique Tarahumara, the catalog's main source, is the same lect. Burgess 1984 p. 8 notes that Brambila and Lionnet describe the Central dialect.
